opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this question from the perspective of someone who builds models but also sits close to the hardware and infrastructure side, so my view might be a little different.

In the short term, it looks like a race on one axis: who has the biggest model, the best benchmark numbers, the most impressive demo. Over the long term, I don't think it stays that simple. A few things will shape how it evolves.

First, the core capability of large language models will become more of a commodity. When many strong teams have access to similar data, similar compute, and similar architectures, the gap at the frontier narrows. We've already seen that once one lab shows something is possible, others reproduce it within months. So pure model quality, by itself, becomes a weaker moat over time.

Second, the competition shifts to the parts that are harder to copy. One is data, especially data that isn't freely available on the internet, like interaction data, domain data, and physical world data. Another is the full system: inference efficiency, cost per token, reliability, and how well the model plugs into real products and workflows. A third is distribution, meaning who already owns the relationship with users or enterprises.

Third, and this is the part I personally care about most, the frontier itself will move. Language was the first domain where scaling worked spectacularly, because the internet gave us an enormous amount of text. But much of the economic value in the world involves the physical world: manufacturing, logistics, driving, robotics. To get AI there, you need models that understand physics, space, and cause and effect, what people call world models or physical AI. That's a much less mature area, and I think a lot of the next decade's competition will happen there. Companies that are strong in language today aren't automatically ahead in that space.

So my guess is that we'll end up with a small number of very large general foundation model providers, because training at the frontier is just extremely expensive. Around them there will be a large ecosystem of companies that specialize, fine-tune, and build on top, often using open models. Open models will play a big role, because many industries want control, customization, and the ability to run things on their own infrastructure.

I also don't think it's winner-take-all. AI is more like electricity or computing than a single product. There's room for many players at different layers. The ones who win long term will be those that keep pushing toward new capabilities instead of only optimizing what already works, and those that can turn capability into something people actually rely on every day.

r001.rationale: The response says that as strong teams gain access to similar resources, the gap at the frontier narrows and model quality becomes a weaker moat.

r002.rationale: It says differentiation will shift to harder-to-copy data, system efficiency and reliability, product integration, and distribution.

r003.rationale: It does not say that a provider’s current lead buys it more time to develop differentiation.

r004.rationale: It does not use the historical spread of software-development capability as an analogy.

r005.rationale: It does not compare AI models to traditional Chinese medicine or describe black-box experimentation building a body of knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question, so let me try to answer it from where I sit, which is on the generative and physical AI side at NVIDIA.

I think the first thing to say is that the frontier is a very crowded place right now, and I don't think it stays that crowded. Training the very largest general-purpose models is becoming enormously capital intensive. Every generation costs more, the data is harder to get, and the returns per dollar on pure scale are no longer as obvious as they were a few years ago. So over the long run I expect only a handful of players will keep competing at the absolute frontier of general models. That is just the economics of it.

But I don't think that means the field consolidates into two or three companies and everyone else goes home. I think the opposite happens below the frontier. The capability floor keeps rising, open models keep improving, and the cost of a given level of intelligence keeps collapsing. When that happens, the interesting competition moves away from "who has the biggest model" and toward "who can turn intelligence into something useful in a specific domain." Medicine, manufacturing, autonomous driving, robotics, scientific discovery. Each of those requires data, physics, evaluation, and domain expertise that a general lab doesn't automatically have.

For me personally, the most interesting frontier is physical AI, and this is where I think the long-term competition is going to look quite different from language. With language, the internet gave everyone a shared corpus. With the physical world, there is no equivalent. You cannot scrape the internet to learn how a robot arm should pick up a wet glass or how a car should behave on an icy road at night. You have to generate that data, simulate it, and close the loop with the real world. So the companies that can build world models, high-fidelity simulation, and the data engines around them will have a very durable advantage, because that data moat compounds in a way that text data does not anymore.

The other dynamic I'd point to is that competition and collaboration are going to coexist much more than people expect. The ecosystem needs open models, open tooling, shared benchmarks. Even fierce competitors will keep building on one another's work because the alternative, everyone reinventing everything, is simply too slow and too expensive. I think the healthy long-term equilibrium is a few frontier labs, a very vibrant open ecosystem underneath, and thousands of companies specializing on top of it.

If I had to summarize, I'd say the question of "which company wins AI" is probably the wrong frame. The more likely outcome is that AI becomes infrastructure, like electricity or networking. A small number of companies will supply the core, and the real value and the real competition will be in what gets built on top. And for physical AI in particular, we're still at the very beginning of that story.

r001.rationale: The response says capability floors will rise and intelligence will get cheaper, but it does not predict that competing models will converge in capability.

r002.rationale: It says competition will shift toward turning intelligence into useful domain-specific applications, which require complementary data, expertise, evaluation, and other capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not connect a model’s current lead to giving its provider more time to develop differentiation.

r004.rationale: It does not use the historical spread of software-development capability as an analogy.

r005.rationale: It does not compare AI models to traditional Chinese medicine or describe black-box experimentation accumulating into a body of knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether having the best model today creates a lasting advantage. You can be ahead at one moment, but if other companies catch up quickly, you have to keep investing just to maintain that position.

Over the long term, I would expect competition to happen on several dimensions: model capability, cost, reliability, and how useful the model is for a particular task. Different customers will value those things differently, so there may be room for multiple winners.

And the model is only part of the product. How do you bring it into someone’s workflow? How do you learn from their feedback and make it more useful? Those things could become very important advantages. So I wouldn’t assume that the company with the strongest model at any particular moment will necessarily be the company that captures the most value over time.

r001.rationale: It says competitors may catch up quickly, but does not clearly predict that model capabilities will gradually converge.

r002.rationale: It says the model is only part of the product and points to workflow integration and learning from feedback as potential advantages.

r003.rationale: It discusses a current lead and ongoing investment, but does not say that a lead gives the provider more time to develop differentiation.

r004.rationale: It makes no analogy to the historical spread of software-development capability.

r005.rationale: It does not compare AI models to traditional Chinese medicine or describe black-box experimentation building shared knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think competition will happen at several layers. At the frontier, training the strongest models requires enormous investment in compute, data, and research, so there may be relatively few companies competing there. But that doesn’t mean only a few companies can build valuable AI businesses.

As models become more capable and less expensive, more of the competition will shift toward what you do with them. Can you solve a particular customer’s problem? Can you make the system reliable, integrate it into their workflow, and deliver it at a reasonable cost? A model that leads on a benchmark doesn’t automatically win on those dimensions.

Open models will also play an important role. They give developers and enterprises more choices, and they put pressure on companies to keep improving both performance and price.

So I wouldn’t assume this becomes a winner-take-all market. You could have some concentration at the frontier and a much broader ecosystem around it. The key uncertainty is how durable any technical advantage will be. If others can catch up quickly, companies will need more than a better model to sustain their position.

r001.rationale: The response says models may become more capable and less expensive and that others might catch up quickly, but it does not predict that competing models will gradually converge in capability.

r002.rationale: It says competition will shift toward solving customer problems, making systems reliable, integrating them into workflows, and delivering them affordably—offerings beyond model capability that can differentiate providers.

r003.rationale: It notes that a benchmark lead does not guarantee broader success and raises uncertainty about technical advantage, but does not say a current lead gives the provider more time to differentiate.

r004.rationale: The response does not use the historical spread of software-development capability as an analogy.

r005.rationale: The response does not compare AI models to traditional Chinese medicine or describe black-box experimentation producing a body of knowledge.
